title: My AI-assisted games with art generated locally on an RTX 5090 are making real money with zero ad spend
author: DesignerGlad6784
selftext:
I've been experimenting with AI game development for a while. My first attempt was about a year ago. It took me around a month, and I still ended up finishing most of it by hand. Back then AI was more of a smart autocomplete than anything else.

At the start of this summer I decided to give it another try, and the result was an order of magnitude better.

This time I didn't want to make another simple puzzle game. Puzzles are probably the easiest thing to build this way, but every idea I came up with felt like something I had already seen 100 times before.

So I spent more time and made games I'd actually find interesting myself: proper graphics, longer gameplay, progression, and a bit more depth.

All the graphics are generated on my own PC with an RTX 5090, running ComfyUI. I didn't use any online image generators.

This mattered more than I expected. I wasn't paying for credits or subscriptions, so I could make as many variations of sprites, backgrounds and UI elements as I needed. I kept going until the art style looked consistent across the whole game, instead of settling for whatever came out first.

It definitely took more effort than just prompting an AI and publishing whatever came out. I spent quite a bit of time iterating, fixing things, changing the gameplay and trying to make them feel like actual games rather than AI demos.

Eventually I published them through Playgama to see if people would actually play them.

And surprisingly, they started making money.

Most of the revenue is coming from YouTube Playables, Playgama, Microsoft Store and Xiaomi. I haven't spent anything on user acquisition, so all of this is coming from organic traffic on those platforms.

Obviously this isn't life-changing money, but I find it pretty cool that games I started as AI experiments are now bringing in actual revenue.

Now I'm working on the next one and trying to understand if I can make this repeatable.

comments.author: OriginlessGamer
comments.body:
I checked 3/4 games (couldn't find Huntsman), the art looks solid. How do you approach your game ideas, mechanics and timelines? Do you prepare a draft of features and concepts in advance or do you straight up start cooking and fixing things along the way?

I have a bunch of ideas myself, but they dry up too quickly after a certain prototype stage, it takes an extra level of insanity to push it beyond this line xD

replies.author: DesignerGlad6784
replies.body:
First I work the idea out "on paper" — I use speech-to-text and just talk out everything that comes to mind about the game. No structure, just getting all the ideas into one pile of text. Then I feed that whole dump straight into an agent.

From there it's a single one-shot prompt to build an MVP.

Once I can actually play it, I go back and fix the mechanics that didn't feel right, and dig deeper into the concept now that I've seen it running.

And after that it's just many, many small iterations to push it to a production state.

The voice dump stage is what keeps me from drying out early, I think — by the time I have a prototype I already know where the idea is supposed to go, so it's less "what now?" and more "just keep grinding."

replies.author: OriginlessGamer
replies.body:
I tried this approach a few times on a "blank project" and the shit that came out of it made me more demoralized about the whole thing than it made me motivated to continue it, hahah

Some of these attempts were games, while other were apps, but unless I truly understand what I'm doing, I feel absolutely powerless about what the AI is cooking, and the more it's doing so, the less I understand how to even debug it properly

But great that it works for you, it can probably be a really solid strategy if you're getting it right (I probably don't xD) 

Anyway, thanks for sharing and keep cooking, you're doing great!
